# Acme Health AI Evaluation and Measurement Standard

## 1. Purpose and Scope

This Standard establishes the requirements for evaluating and measuring the risks and trustworthiness characteristics of AI systems operated by Acme Health. It applies to all AI systems in development, testing, and production at Acme Health, and to all measurement, testing, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) activities performed against those systems across the AI lifecycle.

## 2. Roles and Responsibilities

AI / ML Engineering owns the AI evaluation and measurement process described in this Standard end to end, including the selection of metrics, the execution of evaluations, the documentation of results, and the handoffs to other functions. Domain experts, independent assessors, end users, external AI actors, and affected communities participate in individual measurement and consultation steps as specified below, but accountability for the outcome of every step rests with AI / ML Engineering.

## 3. Measurement of AI Risks

### 3.1 Selection and Application of Risk Measurement Approaches

AI / ML Engineering must select and apply approaches, methods, and metrics for measuring AI risks, starting with the most significant risks identified during the map function, and must properly document any risks or trustworthiness characteristics that will not or cannot be measured. [NIST AI RMF Measure 1 | NIST AI RMF Measure 1.1]

NIST suggests, among its 12 actions for Measure 1.1, establishing approaches for detecting, tracking, and measuring known risks, errors, incidents, or negative impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 1]; identifying testing procedures and metrics to demonstrate whether the system is fit for purpose, functioning as claimed, and trustworthy [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 3]; defining acceptable limits for system performance, including course-correction suggestions when the system performs beyond those limits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 4]; identifying transparency metrics and accountability metrics for AI designers, developers, and deployers [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 7]; documenting metric selection criteria, including considered but unused metrics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 8]; monitoring AI system external inputs, including training data, models and components reused from other contexts, and third-party tools and resources [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 9]; reporting metrics to inform assessments of system generalizability and reliability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 10]; assessing and documenting pre- versus post-deployment system performance, including existing and emergent risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 11]; and documenting risks or trustworthiness characteristics identified in the Map function that will not be measured, including justification for non-measurement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 12].

### 3.2 Assessment of Metric Appropriateness and Control Effectiveness

AI / ML Engineering must regularly assess and update the appropriateness of AI metrics and the effectiveness of existing controls, including reports of errors and potential impacts on affected communities. [NIST AI RMF Measure 1.2]

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 1.2, assessing the external validity of all measurements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 1]; assessing the effectiveness of existing metrics and controls on a regular basis throughout the AI system lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 2]; documenting reports of errors, incidents, and negative impacts and assessing the sufficiency and efficacy of existing metrics for repairs and upgrades [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 3]; developing new metrics when existing metrics are insufficient or ineffective [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 4]; developing and utilizing metrics to monitor, characterize, and track external inputs, including third-party tools [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 5]; determining the frequency and scope for sharing metrics and related information with stakeholders and impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 6]; utilizing stakeholder feedback processes established in the Map function to capture, act upon, and share feedback from end users and potentially impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 7]; and collecting and reporting software quality metrics such as rates of bug occurrence and severity, time to response, and time to repair [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 8].

### 3.3 Independent and Expert Involvement in Assessments

Regular assessments and updates must involve internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers for the system and/or independent assessors, with domain experts, users, external AI actors, and affected communities consulted as necessary per organizational risk tolerance. [NIST AI RMF Measure 1.3]

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 1.3, utilizing separate testing teams to enable independent decisions and course-correction for AI systems, with processes tracked and changes in performance measured and documented [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 2]; planning and evaluating AI system prototypes with end user populations early and continuously in the AI lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 3]; assessing the independence and stature of TEVV and oversight AI actors to ensure they have the required levels of independence and resources to perform assurance, compliance, and feedback tasks effectively [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 4]; evaluating the effectiveness of external stakeholder feedback mechanisms for eliciting, evaluating, and integrating input from diverse groups and for enhancing AI actor visibility and decision making regarding AI system risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 7]; and identifying and utilizing participatory approaches for assessing impacts that may arise from changes in system deployment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 8].

## 4. Evaluation of Trustworthy Characteristics

### 4.1 Trustworthiness Evaluation and TEVV Documentation

AI / ML Engineering must evaluate AI systems for trustworthy characteristics, with test sets, metrics, and details about the tools used during TEVV documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2 | NIST AI RMF Measure 2.1]

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Measure 2.1, leveraging existing industry best practices for transparency and documentation of all possible aspects of measurements, such as data sheets for data sets and model cards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 1]; regularly assessing the effectiveness of tools used to document measurement approaches, test sets, metrics, processes, and materials used [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 2]; and updating those tools as needed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 3].

### 4.2 Human Subject Evaluations

Evaluations involving human subjects must meet applicable requirements, including human subject protection, and must be representative of the relevant population. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.2]

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 2.2, following human subjects research requirements, including informed consent and compensation, during dataset collection activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 1]; analyzing differences between the intended and actual population of users or data subjects [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 2]; utilizing disaggregated evaluation methods, for example by race, age, gender, ethnicity, ability, or region [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 3]; establishing thresholds and alert procedures for dataset representativeness within the context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 4]; following intellectual property and privacy rights related to datasets and their use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 6]; evaluating data representativeness through investigation of known failure modes, assessment of data quality and diverse sourcing, application of public benchmarks, traditional bias testing, chaos engineering, and stakeholder feedback [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 7]; and using informed consent for individuals providing data used in system testing and evaluation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 8].

### 4.3 Performance and Assurance Criteria in Deployment-Like Conditions

AI system performance or assurance criteria must be measured qualitatively or quantitatively and demonstrated for conditions similar to the deployment setting(s), with the measures documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.3]

NIST suggests, among its 9 actions for Measure 2.3, conducting regular and sustained engagement with potentially impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 1]; regularly testing and evaluating systems in non-optimized conditions in collaboration with AI actors in user interaction and user experience roles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 3]; measuring AI systems prior to deployment in conditions similar to expected scenarios [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 6]; measuring and documenting performance criteria such as validity (false positive rate, false negative rate) and efficiency (training times, prediction latency) related to ground truth within the deployment context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 7]; measuring assurance criteria such as AI actor competency and experience [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 8]; and documenting differences between the measurement setting and the deployment environment(s) [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 9].

### 4.4 Production Monitoring of Functionality and Behavior

The functionality and behavior of the AI system and its components, as identified in the map function, must be monitored when in production through the [Monitoring System]. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.4]

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Measure 2.4, monitoring and documenting how metrics and performance indicators observed in production differ from those collected during pre-deployment testing, considering error propagation and feedback loop risks when differences are observed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 1]; monitoring for anomalies using approaches such as control limits, confidence intervals, integrity constraints, and ML algorithms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 3]; verifying that alerts are in place for when distributions in new input data or generated predictions differ from pre-deployment test outcomes, or when anomalies are detected [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 4]; assessing the accuracy and quality of generated outputs against newly collected ground-truth information as it becomes available [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 5]; and utilizing human review to track processing of unexpected data and reliability of generated outputs, warning system users when outputs may be unreliable, and verifying that human overseers have clearly defined responsibilities and training [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 6].

### 4.5 Validity, Reliability, and Generalizability

The AI system to be deployed must be demonstrated to be valid and reliable, and limitations of its generalizability beyond the conditions under which it was developed must be documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.5]

NIST suggests, among its 15 actions for Measure 2.5, establishing or identifying and documenting approaches to measure forms of validity, including construct, internal, and external validity [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 3]; assessing and documenting system variance using standard approaches such as confidence intervals, standard deviation, standard error, bootstrapping, or cross-validation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 4]; establishing or identifying and documenting robustness measures and reliability measures [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 6]; monitoring operating conditions for system performance outside of defined limits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 11]; defining post-alert actions, such as alerting relevant AI actors, requesting human review, alerting downstream users and stakeholders, tracking and mitigating error propagation, and action logging [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 13]; logging input data and relevant system configuration information whenever there is an attempt to use the system beyond its well-defined range of system validity [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 14]; and modifying the system over time to extend its range of system validity to new operating conditions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 15].

### 4.6 Safety Evaluation

The AI system must be evaluated regularly for safety risks identified in the map function; the system to be deployed must be demonstrated to be safe, its residual negative risk must not exceed the risk tolerance, and it must be able to fail safely — particularly if operated beyond its knowledge limits — with safety metrics reflecting system reliability and robustness, real-time monitoring, and response times for AI system failures. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.6]

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Measure 2.6, thoroughly measuring system performance in development and deployment contexts and under stress conditions, including stress-testing under likely scenarios such as concept drift and high load, testing under conditions similar to past known incidents or near-misses, applying chaos engineering approaches, and documenting the range of conditions under which the system has been demonstrated to fail safely [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 1]; measuring and monitoring system performance in real-time to enable rapid response when AI system incidents are detected [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 2]; collecting pertinent safety statistics such as out-of-range performance, incident response times, and system down time [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 3]; documenting, practicing, and measuring incident response plans for AI system incidents, including measuring response and down times [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 5]; and comparing documented safety testing and monitoring information with established risk tolerances on an ongoing basis [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 6].

### 4.7 Security and Resilience Evaluation

AI system security and resilience, as identified in the map function, must be evaluated and documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.7]

NIST suggests, among its 10 actions for Measure 2.7, establishing and tracking AI system security tests and metrics, such as red-teaming activities, frequency and rate of anomalous events, system down-time, incident response times, and time-to-bypass [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 1]; using red-team exercises to actively test the system under adversarial or stress conditions and to evaluate potential mismatches between claimed and actual system performance [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 4]; documenting red-team exercise results as part of continuous improvement efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 3]; using countermeasures such as authentication, throttling, differential privacy, and robust ML approaches to increase the range of security conditions under which the system can return to normal function [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 5]; verifying that third-party AI resources and personnel undergo security audits and screenings [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 9]; and utilizing watermarking technologies as a deterrent to data and model extraction attacks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 10].

### 4.8 Transparency and Accountability Risks

Risks associated with transparency and accountability, as identified in the map function, must be examined and documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.8]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 2.8, instrumenting the system for measurement and tracking, for example by maintaining histories, audit logs, and other information usable by AI actors to review and evaluate possible sources of error, bias, or vulnerability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 1]; testing provided explanations for calibration with different audiences, including operators, end users, decision makers, and decision subjects, to enable recourse for consequential system decisions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 3]; measuring and documenting human oversight of AI systems, including the degree of oversight provided, statistics about downstream actions such as system overrides, and statistics about reported errors or complaints, time to respond, and response types [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 4]; tracking, documenting, and measuring organizational accountability via policy exceptions and escalations and documenting "go" and "no/go" decisions made by accountable parties [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 5]; and tracking and auditing the effectiveness of organizational mechanisms related to AI risk management, including lines of communication, roles and responsibilities, and organizational accountability roles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 6].

### 4.9 Explainability, Validation, and Interpretation of Output

The AI model must be explained, validated, and documented, and AI system output must be interpreted within its context — as identified in the map function — to inform responsible use and governance. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.9]

NIST suggests, among its 11 actions for Measure 2.9, verifying that systems are developed to produce explainable models, post-hoc explanations, and audit logs [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 1]; documenting AI model details including model type, data features, training algorithms, proposed uses, decision thresholds, training data, evaluation data, and ethical considerations [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 4]; establishing, documenting, and reporting performance and error metrics across demographic groups and other segments relevant to the deployment context [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 5]; explaining systems using a variety of methods and testing explanations according to properties such as fidelity, consistency, robustness, and interpretability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 6]; assessing the characteristics of system explanations according to properties such as fidelity, ambiguity, interpretability, interactivity, consistency, and resilience to attack or manipulation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 7]; testing the quality of system explanations with end users and other groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 8]; and using transparency tools such as data statements and model cards to document explanatory and validation information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 11].

### 4.10 Privacy Risk Examination

Privacy risk of the AI system, as identified in the map function, must be examined and documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.10]

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 2.10, documenting the collection, use, management, and disclosure of personally sensitive information in datasets in accordance with privacy and data governance policies [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 2]; quantifying privacy-level data aspects such as the ability to identify individuals or groups, for example using k-anonymity metrics, l-diversity, and t-closeness [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 3]; establishing and documenting protocols (authorization, duration, type) and access controls for training sets or production data containing personally sensitive information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 4]; monitoring internal queries to production data for detecting patterns that isolate personal records [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 5]; and using privacy-enhancing techniques such as differential privacy when publicly sharing dataset information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 7].

### 4.11 Fairness and Bias Evaluation

Fairness and bias, as identified in the map function, must be evaluated and the results documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.11]

NIST suggests, among its 24 actions for Measure 2.11, conducting fairness assessments that identify types of harms, identify across, within, and intersecting groups that might be harmed, quantify harms using general and context-specific fairness metrics, and analyze quantified harms for contextually significant differences [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 1]; using context-specific fairness metrics to examine how system performance varies across groups, within groups, and for intersecting groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 7]; defining acceptable levels of difference in performance in accordance with established organizational governance policies, business requirements, regulatory compliance, legal frameworks, and ethical standards within the context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 9]; defining the actions to be taken if disparity levels rise above acceptable levels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 10]; monitoring system outputs for performance or bias issues that exceed established tolerance levels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 13]; and evaluating practices along the lifecycle to identify potential sources of human-cognitive bias such as availability, observational, and confirmation bias [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 22].

### 4.12 Environmental Impact and Sustainability

The environmental impact and sustainability of AI model training and management activities, as identified in the map function, must be assessed and documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.12]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 2.12, identifying and implementing key indicators of AI system energy and water consumption, efficiency, and/or GHG emissions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 2]; establishing measurable baselines for sustainable AI system operation in accordance with organizational policies, regulatory compliance, legal frameworks, and environmental protection and sustainability norms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 3]; identifying and establishing acceptable resource consumption, efficiency, and GHG emissions levels, along with actions to be taken if indicators rise above acceptable levels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 5]; and estimating AI system emissions levels throughout the AI lifecycle via carbon calculators or a similar process [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 6].

### 4.13 Effectiveness of TEVV Metrics and Processes

The effectiveness of the employed TEVV metrics and processes in the measure function must be evaluated and documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 2.13]

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Measure 2.13, reviewing selected system metrics and associated TEVV processes to determine if they are able to sustain system improvements, including the identification and removal of errors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 1]; regularly evaluating system metrics for utility and considering descriptive approaches in place of overly complex methods [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 2]; reviewing selected system metrics for acceptability within the end user and impacted community of interest [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 3]; and assessing the effectiveness of metrics for identifying and measuring risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 4].

## 5. Identification and Tracking of AI Risks

### 5.1 Ongoing Risk Identification and Tracking

AI / ML Engineering must maintain approaches, personnel, and documentation to regularly identify and track existing, unanticipated, and emergent AI risks based on factors such as intended and actual performance in deployed contexts. [NIST AI RMF Measure 3 | NIST AI RMF Measure 3.1]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 3.1, comparing AI system risks with simpler or traditional models, human baseline performance, and other manual performance benchmarks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 1]; comparing end user and community feedback about deployed AI systems to internal measures of system performance [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 2]; assessing the effectiveness of metrics for identifying and measuring emergent risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 3]; measuring error response times and tracking response quality [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 4]; and eliciting and tracking feedback from AI actors in user support, incident response, and support roles about the type of metrics, explanations, and other system information required for fulsome resolution of system issues, and about the adequacy of staffing and resources to perform their duties effectively and in a timely manner [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 6].

### 5.2 Risk Tracking Where Metrics Are Not Available

Risk tracking approaches must be considered for settings where AI risks are difficult to assess using currently available measurement techniques or where metrics are not yet available. [NIST AI RMF Measure 3.2]

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Measure 3.2, establishing processes for tracking emergent risks that may not be measurable with current approaches, including recourse mechanisms for faulty AI system outputs, bug bounties, human-centered design approaches, user-interaction and experience research, and participatory stakeholder engagement with affected or potentially impacted individuals and communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 1]; identifying AI actors responsible for tracking emergent risks and inventorying methods [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 2]; and determining and documenting the rate of occurrence and severity level for complex or difficult-to-measure risks when prioritizing new measurement approaches, allocating AI system risk management resources, evaluating AI system improvements, and making go/no-go decisions for subsequent system iterations [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 3].

### 5.3 Feedback and Appeal Processes

Feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes must be established through the [Ticketing System] and integrated into AI system evaluation metrics. [NIST AI RMF Measure 3.3]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 3.3, measuring the efficacy of end user and operator error reporting processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 1]; categorizing and analyzing the type and rate of end user appeal requests and results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 2]; measuring feedback activity participation rates and awareness of feedback activity availability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 3]; utilizing feedback to analyze measurement approaches and determine subsequent courses of action [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 4]; evaluating measurement approaches to determine efficacy for enhancing organizational understanding of real-world impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 5]; and analyzing end user and community feedback in close collaboration with domain experts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 6].

## 6. Contextual Measurement and Validation

### 6.1 Connection of Measurement Approaches to Deployment Context

Measurement approaches for identifying AI risks must be connected to deployment context(s), informed through consultation with domain experts and other end users, and documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 4 | NIST AI RMF Measure 4.1]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.1, supporting mechanisms for capturing feedback from system end users, including domain experts, operators, and practitioners, conducted in settings where end users can openly share their doubts and insights about AI system output in connection to their specific context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 1]; identifying and documenting approaches for evaluating and integrating elicited feedback from system end users, in collaboration with human-factors and socio-technical domain experts, to actively inform a process of continual improvement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 2]; utilizing end user feedback to investigate how selected metrics and measurement approaches interact with organizational and operational contexts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 4]; and identifying and implementing approaches to measure effectiveness and satisfaction with end user elicitation techniques, and documenting results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 6].

### 6.2 Validation of Trustworthiness Results in Deployment Contexts

Measurement results regarding AI system trustworthiness in deployment context(s) and across the AI lifecycle must be informed by input from domain experts and relevant AI actors to validate whether the system is performing consistently as intended, and the results must be documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 4.2]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.2, integrating feedback from end users, operators, and affected individuals and communities from the Map function as inputs to assess AI system trustworthiness characteristics, ensuring both positive and negative feedback is assessed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 1]; evaluating feedback regarding end user satisfaction with, and confidence in, AI system performance, including whether output is considered valid, reliable, explainable, and interpretable [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 3]; measuring the frequency of AI systems' override decisions, evaluating and documenting results, and feeding insights back into continual improvement processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 5]; and consulting AI actors in impact assessment, human factors, and socio-technical tasks to assist with analysis and interpretation of results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 6].

### 6.3 Identification of Performance Improvements and Declines

Measurable performance improvements or declines — based on consultations with relevant AI actors, including affected communities, and field data about context-relevant risks and trustworthiness characteristics — must be identified and documented. [NIST AI RMF Measure 4.3]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.3, developing baseline quantitative measures for trustworthy characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 1]; delimiting and characterizing baseline operation values and states [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 2]; utilizing qualitative approaches to augment and complement quantitative baseline measures, in close coordination with impact assessment, human factors, and socio-technical AI actors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 3]; monitoring and assessing measurements as part of continual improvement to identify potential system adjustments or modifications [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 4]; performing and documenting sensitivity analysis to characterize actual and expected variance in performance after applying system or procedural updates [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 5]; and documenting decisions related to the sensitivity analysis and recording the expected influence on system performance and identified risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 6].
